opening.headline: As the number of documents increases, you learn how to put them in context and where to start searching, and how to compare and select the three structures based on the same criteria.
body: At first, it works fine even if you paste a few documents into the prompt. However, as the number of documents increases, the context window fills up and calls become more expensive. However, creating a search system requires chunking, embedding, indexing, and updating.

In this class, we will first check why RAG is needed, how it works, and why chunk size and overlap are determined. Next, we look at the three structures in turn - long context, managed file search, and build-your-own RAG - and check out the reference architectures presented by cloud providers. Finally, we solve for the reasons why the choices are different in the two scenarios of 100 documents and 100,000 documents.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain why RAG is needed and the operational sequence of search, injection, and creation
Describe the impact of chunk size and overlap on search precision and context preservation
Can explain the differences between long contexts, managed file search, and build-your-own RAGs
It can provide a basis for selecting a structure that suits the number of documents, update cycle, and separation of authority requirements.

screens.title: As the number of documents increases, it becomes more confusing where to put them.
screens.lead: Read along as the document grows. It is a good idea to read it while thinking about the burden that arises at each stage.

visual.alt: A graph where the bar becomes longer as the document volume increases and overlaps the context window capacity line.

paragraphs: Let's say you're building a chatbot that asks questions about company documents. At first, it works fine even if you paste a few documents into the prompt. The structure is simple and there is no separate operating system.

The situation changes as the number of documents increases. The cost increases as the context window fills up and the number of input tokens increases with each call. However, if you create a search system, you must operate chunking, embedding, indexing, and updating to divide the document into pieces.

Ultimately, the question is this: To what extent is a long context sufficient, and where does searching begin? The answer is not determined by size alone. How often documents change and what documents different users can see will influence your choice of different map structures.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Number of documents, update cycle, and viewing rights. If any of these three grows, why should we reconsider the structure? Answer again at the end of class.

screens.outro: Before looking at all three options on the same set of documents, let's first recall your own experience.

screens.title: think about it
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever wanted to have AI read your company documents and answer questions?
items.answer: This need exists in almost every organization. Implementation methods range from inserting the entire document to selecting fragments through search. The size and nature of the document determines the method.

items.prompt: What happens to index updates in an environment where documents change dozens of times a day?
items.answer: If the indexed content is not updated, answers will be based on outdated documents. The shorter the refresh cycle, the more important index pipelines and update automation become. On the other hand, the whole method uses the document at the time of request, so the update problem is simple.

items.prompt: What happens if each department uses documents with different viewing rights in one search box?
items.answer: If you do not distinguish between permissions, the contents of documents that cannot be viewed may be mixed in the answer. The search structure requires a design that divides the search scope with attribute filters according to user permissions.

screens.outro: The three questions serve as a basis for comparing subsequent structures. Let's start with the simplest long context.

screens.title: What is RAG and why is it needed?
screens.lead: Before comparing the three structures, we first check the basic principles of RAG. Select each tab to learn about the limitations of the model, the order in which RAGs operate, and why chunk sizes and overlaps are determined.

tabs.label: What the model doesn't know
tabs.body:
A language model's knowledge comes from the data it sees when learning. So there are two limitations. We are not aware of information created after learning or private documents that only exist within our organization. And you can give plausible answers even to things you don’t know.

You might think that it would be possible to retrain the model, but this is expensive and cannot be done every time the document changes. Therefore, a method is used to include the necessary knowledge in the prompt at the moment a question is asked. This method is RAG.

tabs.label: Search, Inject, Create
tabs.body:
Search Augmentation Generation (RAG) works in three steps:

1. **Search**: Find document fragments in external storage that are relevant to your question.
2. **Inject**: Insert the found fragment into the prompt with a question.
3. **Generate**: The model creates an answer based on what is entered in the prompt.

The 2020 RAG paper proposed this structure as a framework for combining the knowledge contained in model weights with an external, searchable index. The advantage is that when knowledge changes, you only need to update the external index without having to retrain the model, and you can point to which fragment the answer was based on.

tabs.label: chunk size
tabs.body:
Documents are not indexed as a whole, but divided into pieces called chunks. Chunk size is a trade-off between search precision and context preservation.

- **If too large**: Multiple topics are mixed in one chunk, resulting in blurred vectors and inaccurate distances from the query. Even when entering it in the prompt, tokens are wasted by including unnecessary information.
- **If it is too small**: Even if you look for it precisely, it becomes a meaningless piece because there is no context. For example, the snippet “Sales increased 3% from the previous quarter” does not tell you which quarter for which company.

Since the appropriate size varies depending on the nature of the document, it is checked and adjusted using a set of predetermined queries.

tabs.label: overlap
tabs.body:
Mechanically cutting chunks to a given size can cause a sentence or paragraph to split in two at a boundary. If the content needed for the answer is split into two chunks, neither of which is close enough to the query, it's easy to miss in a search.

If adjacent chunks are cut so that some of their content overlaps, the bordered content will fit completely into at least one chunk. The trade-off is that there is more to store and embed, and similar chunks can be retrieved together due to overlapping content. Cutting at the boundaries of the document structure, such as paragraphs or headings, may reduce the need for overlap.

screens.outro: Now that you know the principle, let's start with the simplest way to insert the entire document.

ext.title: Lewis et al., Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks

screens.title: Method 1: Long Context
screens.lead: We take a step-by-step look at how the long context method works and how far it works. Select the right arrow to follow the document as it populates the window, caches are applied, and limits are applied.

visual.alt: Illustration of documents populating the context window one after another, with the Apply Cache indicator turned on.
labels: Space shared by input, thinking, and output

steps.title: 1. Put everything in
steps.body: The long context approach involves putting the entire knowledge base into a prompt and asking questions. There is no need for a search system, and the model can view the entire document at once. There is a notice that if the document is less than about 200,000 tokens (about 500 pages), you can put it all in the prompt and no RAG is needed. However, entering the window and having the model write the contents accurately are two different issues, so continue to check in step 4 below.

steps.title: 2. You can use a large window
steps.body: The Gemini documentation explains that many Gemini models have windows of 1 million tokens or more. When the window was small, it was necessary to save tokens by discarding or summarizing old messages, using RAG and vector databases, or filtering prompts, but with a large window, it is said that access to directly providing related information all at once became possible.

steps.title: 3. Reduce recurring costs with caching
steps.body: Using prompt caching or context caching reduces the cost and delay of repeating large inputs. Anthropic explains that prompt caching can more than double delays and reduce costs by up to 90 percent. For services that ask questions to the same document multiple times, whether or not to apply caching greatly determines the cost.

steps.title: 4. A window is a shared space.
steps.body:
A window is a space shared between input, thinking, and output. Larger inputs may result in less output headroom. Getting into the window doesn't always give you a sufficient answer.

Another thing is that the information included is not written equally well in all locations. The Lost in the Middle study reported that in long inputs, models tend to be noticeably less accurate when relevant information is in the middle rather than at the beginning or end. The same trend is said to have appeared in models with long windows. So, rather than just deciding that "entering the window is enough," you should check whether you answer accurately even when important information is in the middle of input.

steps.title: 5. Limitations
steps.body: If the number of documents continues to grow, it will eventually exceed the window, and if only some documents need to be shown for each permission, inserting all of them is not appropriate. In this case, a structure is needed to select only the necessary pieces through search.

screens.outro: Next is managed file search, where the provider does the searching for you.

ext.title: Liu et al., Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts

screens.title: Method 2: Managed file search
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare how the three services work from upload to query. Pay attention to what part I will implement.

tabs.label: OpenAI file search
tabs.body: If you upload a file to the vector store, it is a hosting tool that searches for a model when you need it through semantic search and keyword search. Chunking, embedding, and indexing are not performed directly. You can narrow your results with metadata or attribute filters.

tabs.label: Gemini File Search
tabs.body: Take data, chunk it, and index it. According to the documentation, embedding costs only when indexing, and embedding at storage and query time is free. For services with many inquiries, this cost structure becomes an important decision basis. This service also allows you to narrow your results with metadata.

tabs.label: Snowflake Cortex Search
tabs.body: We configure a hybrid search engine combining vectors and keywords in a matter of minutes, and take care of embedding, infrastructure maintenance, and index updates. If your data is already in Snowflake and frequently updated, the advantage is that you can leave the renewals to the service. The column you specified as `ATTRIBUTES` when creating the service can be used as a filter in the query, narrowing the results by, for example, the Region column. The permissions for the service itself are controlled by granting `USAGE` to the role.

tabs.label: What I will implement
tabs.body: For all three services, chunking, embedding, and indexing are handled by the provider. The code I will implement is reduced to uploading, calling the query, and using the results. The biggest advantage is a shorter development period and fewer systems to operate. Instead, detailed control, such as chunking method or search algorithm, is limited to what the service allows. Therefore, it is a good idea to check in advance whether the service's chunking method matches the nature of your document (whether it has many tables or long paragraphs).

screens.outro: This time, we will look at the configuration of assembling all the steps yourself.

screens.title: Method 3: Build your own RAG with chunking and re-ranking
screens.lead: If you select the number marker above the picture, the roles and options for each stage of the pipeline will appear. Please check them one by one starting from number 1.

visual.alt: Schematic diagram of the RAG pipeline leading to document segmentation, embedding, vector storage, search, re-ranking, and prompt combining.

markers.label: chunking
markers.title: Divide your knowledge base into small chunks
markers.body: Divide your knowledge base into chunks of a few hundred tokens or less. If the chunks are too large, you'll end up with irrelevant content, and if the chunks are too small, context will be lost. Chunks are sometimes cut with some overlap to prevent content from splitting at the border. Contextual Retrieval reduces the problem of search failure due to loss of context due to chunking by prepending 50 to 100 tokens of explanatory context to each chunk. Anthropic's article reports that using context-enhanced embeddings in combination with BM25 reduced search failures by reducing the percentage of correct chunks not in the top 20 from 5.7% to 2.9% (a 49% reduction).

markers.label: Embedding
markers.title: Convert chunks to vectors
markers.body: Create a vector for each chunk with the embedding model. Search quality and storage costs vary depending on which model you use and how many dimensions it has. If the document is modified, the vectors for that chunk must also be recreated.

markers.label: vector store
markers.title: Store and index vectors
markers.body: Place the created vector into the vector storage. The repository maintains an index to quickly find chunks close to the query vector. What kind of storage to use and how to merge it with the existing database are the parts I decide when building.

markers.label: search
markers.title: Find chunks close to the query
markers.body: Embed the user's query to find meaningful chunks and paste the top results into the prompt. You can control how many to import, how to filter them, and whether to mix them with your keyword search.

markers.label: re-ranking
markers.title: Reorder the candidates
markers.body: Re-ranking is a step to increase precision by rearranging the candidates collected through search. For the first search, the query and document are created as separate vectors, and the document vector is calculated in advance and only the distance is compared, allowing you to quickly scan through many documents. Instead, the fine-grained relationships between queries and documents are each compressed into one vector, resulting in loss. The re-ranking model is more precise because it reads the query and candidate documents together as one input and determines the degree of relatedness by looking at each other's words, but it is slow because the model must be run for each candidate. So, we first select candidates through a quick search and then apply re-ranking to only a small number of candidates. Contextual Retrieval reports that adding reranking reduced the failure rate for the same metric by 1.9% (a 67% reduction), so it performed best in a setting where the first 150 candidates were narrowed down to 20. The advantage of building your own is that you can tailor these steps to fit your data.

screens.outro: Let's continue with the reference architecture provided by the cloud provider.

ext.title: Nogueira & Cho, Passage Re-ranking with BERT

screens.title: RAG engine and reference architecture
screens.lead: If you hover over or select an underlined term in the text, an explanation will appear. Check them one by one and connect them to your selection criteria.

data.text: Google Cloud documentation organizes the core concepts of RAG in the order of data collection, transformation, embedding, indexing, retrieval, and generation. RAG Engine is a component that enhances a model's context with external data, reducing hallucination and improving accuracy. The Architecture Center includes various reference architectures such as one based on vector search (Fully managed configuration) and another that combines vectors with operational data in AlloyDB. The selection of architecture depends on factors such as scale, latency, utilization of existing databases, and operational burden.

terms.tip: A component that augments the model's context with external data to reduce hallucinations and increase accuracy. We provide steps from collection to creation.
This is a phenomenon in which a model makes groundless information plausible. You can reduce this by putting the searched evidence into context.
It is based on vector search and leaves the operational burden to the provider. Perfect for getting started quickly.
This is an example of a configuration that puts vectors in the same database as operational data. Select when you want to utilize an existing database.

It's the work that goes into running a structure, like updating indexes, responding to failures, and managing costs. Comparisons are made with scale, latency, and existing database utilization as one of the selection criteria.

screens.outro: Now that we've looked at all the structures, let's explain the choices with examples. First, if there are 100 documents.

screens.title: Explanation: Selection when there are 100 documents
screens.lead: The instructor checks the scenario of 100 documents against four criteria. Select the arrows to the right to view them in order of size, renewals, entitlements, and costs.

visual.alt: A diagram in which the four inspection cards of scale, renewal, authority, and cost are connected to a conclusion.
labels: Size: Around hundreds of thousands of tokens
Long context + caching, no RAG created

steps.title: 1. Size check
steps.body: Assume that 100 documents total approximately 100,000 tokens (this is a hypothetical example, you will have to count the actual value yourself). There is a guide saying that if it is less than 200,000 tokens, you can put in everything, and there are also models that can use windows with more than 1 million tokens. The scale is the range where long contexts are possible. However, as the larger the input, the output margin may decrease, so it is best to leave some margin so that it does not hit the window's limit. Because the size of the window does not guarantee accuracy, the set of questions also includes questions asking about the middle of the document to ensure accuracy.

steps.title: 2. Update check
steps.body: If updates are once a week, you can simply add the newest document at the time of request. Since there is no need to create a separate index, there is no problem with the index and the original being misaligned.

steps.title: 3. Check permissions
steps.body: Everyone has the same permissions, so there's no need to filter documents by user. There is no need to design attribute filters or access separation.

steps.title: 4. Cost check
steps.body: If the number of questions increases and call costs become an issue, check whether caching is enabled. Since the same document is input every time, the cost depends on whether the cache is applied.

steps.title: 5. Conclusion
steps.body: It is correct not to create RAGs at this scale. The implementation and operational burden is minimal, and there are no quality issues where searches miss relevant pieces. A good design is not to choose a structure that is more complicated than necessary.

steps.title: signal of transition
steps.body: If the number of documents increases and becomes difficult to fit in the window, updates become frequent, or departmental authority arises, it is time to reconsider the structure. The following scenario is exactly that: If you decide in advance when to change the structure, you can do so without panic when your documents grow. For example, set a standard such as considering introducing search when the document volume exceeds half of the window.

screens.outro: Let's compare it with a larger scale example.

ext.title: Liu et al., Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts

screens.title: Explanation: Choices when there are 100,000 documents
screens.lead: The instructor checks the scenario where the number of documents has increased to 100,000 using the same criteria. Select the arrow to the right to see the items to check and the structure to choose.

visual.alt: In the scenario of 100,000 documents, the judgment flow is divided into either managed service or direct deployment depending on the inspection items.
labels: Does it go into the window?
Are updates daily and permissions departmental?
Separate access scope with attribute filters
Get started quickly: Managed File Search or Cortex Search
Fine tuning, combined with existing DB: build your own RAG or reference architecture

steps.title: 1. Size check
steps.body: 100,000 cannot fit in the window. At this scale, inserting the whole thing is impossible, so you have to search to select only the pieces you need.

steps.title: 2. Update and permission check
steps.body: With daily updates, you need automation to keep your index up to date. If the permissions for each department are different, the access range is divided using attribute filters to prevent documents that cannot be viewed by the user from entering the search target.

steps.title: 3. To get started quickly
steps.body: Start with services like Managed File Search or Cortex Search. Since the service takes care of chunking, embedding, and indexing, my implementation is reduced to uploading, calling queries, and using the results. This is ideal when you need to get it to market quickly.

steps.title: 4. If you need detailed control
steps.body: If you need to fine-tune search quality or merge with an existing database, use a home-built RAG or cloud reference architecture. Although the control is large, the operational burden is also large.

steps.title: 5. What you need either way
steps.body: Whichever structure you choose, context enrichment and re-ranking of chunks reduces search failures. This is because if context is lost due to chunking, search will fail.

steps.title: 6. Check the quality
steps.body: Just because it's managed doesn't mean you don't have to check quality. You only have fewer points of control, so check your results with a set of real questions. The reason why the choices of 100 and 100,000 are different is because the three demands of scale, renewal, and authority are different.

screens.outro: Now let's summarize the entire lesson.

screens.title: Scale, renewal, and authority set the structure.
screens.lead: Let's go back to the first question and tie together the judgment criteria for this class.

paragraphs: The first question was how long the context ends and where the search begins. If the document is small, put the entire document into a long context, and if it is large, search for it and put only the necessary pieces. The three criteria for choosing a structure are the number of documents, renewal frequency, and separation of authority requirements.

Managed file search (OpenAI file search, Gemini File Search, Snowflake Cortex Search) can be started quickly, with chunking, embedding, and indexing handled by the provider. Building your own RAG requires a lot of control because you assemble chunking, embedding, vector storage, and re-ranking, but the operational burden is also high.

The problem of context disappearing when chunking is reduced by adjusting chunk size and overlap, contextual retrieval, and re-ranking. Re-ranking reads queries and candidates together to sort them more precisely than the initial search. Even after choosing a structure, we always check the quality with a set of actual questions, and even if the document is large enough to fit in a window, we also include questions asking about the content in intermediate positions to check accuracy.

The three structures are not mutually exclusive. You can always keep a small number of frequently used documents in a long context, and retrieve the remaining large documents through search. Choosing a structure is not a one-time decision, but rather a judgment that is revisited as needs change.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Choose the structure that most simply meets your needs. As your needs grow, you can move up one level at a time. The simpler the structure, the easier it is to find the cause when a problem occurs, and the less expensive it is to fix it. Any choice to complicate the structure must be well-founded.

glossary.def: This method puts many documents directly into the prompt window without searching.
The process of breaking a document into small, searchable pieces. You can reduce problems with content splitting at the border by cutting adjacent pieces so that they overlap some of the content.
It is a search tool where chunking, embedding, and indexing are handled by the provider.

This is the step of rereading search candidates along with the query and sorting them precisely. It is more accurate than the initial search, but is slower, so it is only applied to selected candidates.
This method involves searching for information related to a question, attaching it to a prompt, and having the model answer based on the information.

misconceptions.myth: Once you enter the window, all content can be used equally well regardless of location.
misconceptions.fact: There has been a reported tendency for accuracy to decrease with long inputs when relevant information is interspersed. You must check separately whether it enters the window and whether you answer correctly.

misconceptions.myth: Now that the window is bigger, RAG is no longer needed.
misconceptions.fact: This is true if the document fits into a window, but if it is large or requires updates and separation of rights, searching is still necessary.

misconceptions.myth: Managed file search doesn't require you to worry about quality.
misconceptions.fact: It just reduces the number of points you can adjust. It is still necessary to check the results with a set of actual questions.

misconceptions.myth: No matter how you divide chunking, the result is the same.
misconceptions.fact: Chunks that are too large can blur searches, and chunks that are too small can lose context and cause content to split at the boundaries. Determine size and overlap, and reduce them by enriching context and re-ranking.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: RAG retrieves relevant fragments at question time, puts them in the prompt, and lets the model answer based on the content. All you have to do is update the index when the document changes.
If the document is small, place it entirely in a long context and check for accuracy; if it is large, search for it and include only the necessary pieces.

For managed file searches, the provider takes care of chunking, embedding, and indexing, and for self-built RAGs, I assemble chunking, embedding, vector storage, and re-ranking, so I have a lot of control, but the operational burden is also high.
Number of documents, renewal cycle, and separation of authority requirements are three criteria for choosing a structure.
Chunk size, overlap, context enrichment, and re-ranking reduce the problem of context being lost when chunking.

checks.q: When the chunks were indexed in very large chunks (thousands of tokens), the number of cases where the search results did not match the query increased. What is the best explanation?
options: This is because the larger the chunk, the more multiple topics are mixed in one chunk, making the vector blurry, and unnecessary content is also included in the prompt.
This is because the larger the chunk, the more accurately the embedding model understands the document.
Chunk size is another cause as it does not affect search results
This is because the larger the chunk, the slower the search speed and the more incorrect the results.
checks.explain: Chunk size is a trade-off between precision and context preservation. If it is too large, the distance will be inaccurate because the topic will be mixed, and if it is too small, the context will disappear, so check and adjust it with a collection of queries.

wrong.1: Splitting things up doesn't make the model more accurate; it just mixes up the topics.
wrong.2: Chunk size directly affects search precision and what goes into the prompt.
wrong.3: The problem is not speed, but the mixing of multiple topics in one vector, blurring the meaning.
